paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-123 (DEE123) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. Its main features are developmental delay, hypotonia and seizures, which may be drug-resistant. Some patients also have intellectual disability, microcephaly, failure to thrive, gastroesophageal reflux, and brain MRI anomalies such as cerebral and cerebellar atrophy.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of DEE123 is autosomal recessive. Krami et al. (2022) were the first to report a homozygous HECW2 variant inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Previously reported HECW2 variants had been de novo and heterozygous. In the family reported by Dehghanzad et al. (2025), both parents were unaffected heterozygous carriers of their daughter's homozygous HECW2 variant.

paragraphs.text: In a Caucasian girl with DEE123, Rodríguez-García et al. (2022) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous mutation in the HECW2 gene (g.197092814_197092824delinsC). The mutation disrupted the splice donor site of intron 22. This caused skipping of exon 22 (r.3766_3917+1del) and an in-frame deletion (p.Leu1256_Trp1306del). In functional studies, RNA expression was increased twofold but protein levels were reduced by 60%, suggesting partial loss of function.

paragraphs.text: Dehghanzad et al. (2025) identified a homozygous 1-bp insertion in the HECW2 gene (c.3601_3602insT) in a 6-year-old girl of consanguineous Afghan descent with DEE123. The insertion results in a frameshift and premature termination (Tyr1201LeufsTer7). She had severe microcephaly, hypotonia, failure to thrive, recurrent seizures, global neurodevelopmental delay, and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy on brain MRI. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Both unaffected parents were heterozygous carriers. The authors suggested that the mutation probably leads to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and loss of function.
